newsitem.title: USA: Fitch cuts Cook County Forest Preserve District.
newsitem.headline: Fitch cuts Cook County Forest Preserve District.

text.p: Cook County Forest Preserve District (IL.)'s $11,640,000 general obligation zoo bonds, series 1996 and $14,750,000 general obligation limited tax bonds, series 1996 are rated 'A' by Fitch Investors Service.
Additionally, the district's $20.8 million in outstanding general obligation bonds are downgraded to 'A' from 'AA', reflecting the deterioration of the district's financial position.

Despite current management's efforts to restore financial stability and the district's broad economic and taxable property bases and low direct debt burden, the rating outlook is changed to negative pending the district's adoption of a plan to cure the accumulated fund balance deficit and demonstration of ongoing operating balance.
The current bonds are scheduled for negotiated sale the week of Dec. 9, via a syndicate led by Bear, Stearns & Co., Inc.

The bonds, dated Dec. 1, 1996, are due Dec. 1, 1998-2010. Each series of bonds has a term bond due Dec. 1, 2016. Bonds are subject to optional redemption prior to maturity. Zoo bonds are general obligations of the district, payable from an unlimited tax full faith and credit pledge on all of the district's taxable property.

Limited tax bonds -- unlimited as to rate but limited as to amount by the provisions of the Property Tax Limitation Law -- are general obligations of the district, payable from a full faith and credit pledge on all of the district's taxable property. Zoo bonds are being issued to pay costs of financing certain capital improvement projects at the Brookfield Zoo and pay costs of issuance. Limited tax bonds are being issued to create a reserve for the payment of any cost, liability or loss against the district and finance the acquisition of land and construct, acquire, equip, repair and renovate buildings or other improvements to district property.

The district's overall financial performance weakened during the 1990s as property tax levy reductions, expanding expenditures and deliberate general fund balance drawdowns created operational deficits and negative ending balances. Prior year surpluses that did not exist were budgeted as revenues and planned expenditure cuts never materialized. Moreover, significant financial reporting delays historically have postponed recognition and obscured the extent of the district's financial decline.

Operating results for 1994 were only recently available. While audits for fiscal years 1995 and 1996 (ending Dec. 31) have yet to be completed, reports produced from the district's newly implemented accounting system show an apparent end to the district's operating deficits and some improvement in its deficit general fund balance.

These reports appear to indicate there was a structural deficit during fiscals 1991-1994. Since then, the district has scaled back its expenditures considerably, tightened financial controls and improved operational productivity.

While a fund balance deficit remains, the district has reversed its negative trend of deficit spending, produced positive operating results ending fiscal 1995 and projected similar results ending fiscal 1996.
Direct debt burden is low; the district being coterminous with the county brings the overall debt burden to moderate levels.

The county's diverse economic base includes Chicago and its surrounding suburbs, with census levels at 5.1 million in 1990. Population has been relatively stable, declining by about 6% between the 1970-1990 census, while taxable property base growth has been healthy, averaging 6.1% annual growth since fiscal 1981.
